claims.claim: Neural stem and progenitor cells undergo growth and developmental aberrations upon ZIKV infection, resulting in microcephaly.
claims.source: Studies using the brain organoids, neurospheres, and human pluripotent stem cell-derived brain cells have identified that neural stem and progenitor cells can undergo growth and developmental aberrations upon ZIKV infection, thereby resulting in microcephaly (Tang et al., 2016; Cugola et al., 2016; Garcez et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2016; Cugola et al., 2016; Garcez et al., 2016.

claims.claim: ZIKV infects placental macrophages and trophoblasts, leading to placental insufficiency and injury.
claims.source: Several studies have demonstrated that ZIKV infects placental macrophages and trophoblasts, which leads to placental insufficiency and injury (Quicke et al., 2016; Szaba et al., 2018; Brown et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Quicke et al., 2016; Szaba et al., 2018; Brown et al., 2019.

claims.claim: ZIKV infection disrupts the architecture and function of the placenta by triggering trophoblast apoptosis and vascular endothelial cell damage in mouse pregnancy models.
claims.source: Using the mouse pregnancy models, it has been shown that ZIKV infection disrupts the architecture and function of the placenta by triggering trophoblast apoptosis and vascular endothelial cell damage (Miner et al., 2016; Yockey et al., 2016; Ribeiro et al., 2018; Yockey et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Miner et al., 2016; Yockey et al., 2016; Ribeiro et al., 2018; Yockey et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The placenta can suffer from apoptosis during ZIKV infection.
claims.source: During ZIKV infection, the placenta can suffer from apoptosis (Miner et al., 2016; Yockey et al., 2018), which is a prototype of programmed cell death (PCD) and is crucial for reproduction, embryonic development, immunity, and viral infections.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Miner et al., 2016; Yockey et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Pyroptosis is an innate immune response against intracellular pathogens, featured by cell swelling and the emergence of large bubble-like structures from the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Pyroptosis is an innate immune response against intracellular pathogens, and is featured by cell swelling and the emergence of large bubble-like structures from the plasma membrane that differentiate it from other PCDs (Shi et al., 2017; Jorgensen and Miao, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Shi et al., 2017; Jorgensen and Miao, 2015.

claims.claim: Gasdermin D (GSDMD) is a key pyroptosis executor whose N-terminus domain can bind to membrane lipids, phosphoinositides, and cardiolipin to perforate the membrane.
claims.source: Recent studies have identified gasdermin D (GSDMD) as a key pyroptosis executor, whose N-terminus domain is capable of binding to membrane lipids, phosphoinositides, and cardiolipin in order to perforate the membrane, resulting in the release of cytosolic content (Ding et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2015; Kayagaki et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ding et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2015; Kayagaki et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Gasdermin E (GSDME) was originally identified as a gene related to hearing impairment.
claims.source: Gasdermin E (GSDME), also known as DFNA5, belongs to the same superfamily as GSDMD, and was originally identified as a gene related to hearing impairment (Van Laer et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Van Laer et al., 1998.

claims.claim: GSDME is considered a potential tumor suppressor gene in gastric and hepatocellular carcinomas.
claims.source: GSDME is considered as a potential tumor suppressor gene in several types of cancers, such as gastric and hepatocellular carcinomas (Akino et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Akino et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2020.

claims.claim: GSDME mediates pyroptosis via its activated N-terminus domain that is specifically cleaved by caspase-3 and granzyme B.
claims.source: Recently, it has also been demonstrated to mediate pyroptosis via its activated N-terminus (GSDME-N) domain that is specifically cleaved by caspase-3 and granzyme B (Zhang et al., 2020; Rogers et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2020; Rogers et al., 2017.

claims.claim: GSDME can switch caspase-3-mediated apoptosis to pyroptosis or mediate secondary necrosis after apoptosis.
claims.source: GSDME can switch the caspase-3-mediated apoptosis to pyroptosis or can mediate secondary necrosis after apoptosis (Wang et al., 2017), indicating an extensive crosstalk between apoptosis and GSDME-mediated pyroptosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Dengue virus can induce NLRP3 inflammasome-dependent pyroptosis in human macrophages via C-type lectin 5A, which is critical for dengue hemorrhagic fever.
claims.source: For instance, dengue virus can induce the NLRP3 inflammasome-dependent pyroptosis in human macrophages via the C-type lectin 5A, which is critical for dengue hemorrhagic fever (Wu et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Japanese encephalitis virus enhances pyroptosis of peritoneal macrophages to raise serum interleukin-1α level, promoting viral neuroinvasion and blood-brain-barrier disruption.
claims.source: Japanese encephalitis virus enhances the pyroptosis of peritoneal macrophages to raise the serum interleukin-1α level, which in turn promotes viral neuroinvasion and blood-brain-barrier disruption (Wang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claims.claim: ZIKV induces caspase-1- and GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis of neural progenitor cells that contributes to CZS.
claims.source: Particularly, a recent study demonstrated the effect of ZIKV in inducing the caspase-1- and GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis of neural progenitor cells that contributes to CZS (He et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2020.

claims.claim: ZIKV-infected JEG-3 cells showed evident cell swelling with balloon-like structures originating from the plasma membrane, displaying characteristic pyroptotic cell morphology.
claims.source: Upon ZIKV infection, JEG-3 cells showed evident cell swelling with balloon-like structures originating from the plasma membrane that appears to be distinct from the apoptotic blebbing (Figure 1A), displaying a characteristic pyroptotic cell morphology.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1A showing pyroptotic morphology.

claims.claim: ZIKV-infected JEG-3 cells released lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in an infection time-dependent manner.
claims.source: Along with decreased cell viability, the swelling cells were also found to release lactate dehydrogenase (LDH, an indicator of the lytic cell cytotoxicity) in an infection time-dependent manner, which depicts the rupture and leakage of the plasma membrane (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LDH release data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: ZIKV infection led to the release of the N-terminal domain of GSDME (GSDME-N) in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: To this end, the infected cells were subjected to Western blot analysis, and the results revealed that infection led to the release of the N-terminal domain of GSDME (GSDME-N), whereas no cleavage of GSDMD was observed (Figure 1C), implying that ZIKV infection may induce pyroptosis through GSDME.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1C showing GSDME-N cleavage.

claims.claim: No cleavage of GSDMD was observed in ZIKV-infected JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: To this end, the infected cells were subjected to Western blot analysis, and the results revealed that infection led to the release of the N-terminal domain of GSDME (GSDME-N), whereas no cleavage of GSDMD was observed (Figure 1C), implying that ZIKV infection may induce pyroptosis through GSDME.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1C showing no GSDMD cleavage.

claims.claim: Deletion of GSDME significantly suppressed ZIKV-induced cell swelling in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As expected, deletion of GSDME significantly suppressed the ZIKV-induced cell swelling (Figure 1E) as well as LDH release and the decline of cell viability (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1E showing reduced cell swelling in GSDME-KO cells.

claims.claim: Deletion of GSDME significantly suppressed ZIKV-induced LDH release and decline of cell viability in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As expected, deletion of GSDME significantly suppressed the ZIKV-induced cell swelling (Figure 1E) as well as LDH release and the decline of cell viability (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity data in Figure 1F showing reduced LDH release and improved viability in GSDME-KO cells.

claims.claim: Deletion or overexpression of GSDME did not affect ZIKV replication in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: In addition, to explore whether GSDME-mediated pyroptosis could affect ZIKV replication, the plaque assay was conducted in GSDME-KO and -overexpressed JEG-3 cells, and the results showed that deletion or overexpression of GSDME did not affect ZIKV replication in JEG-3 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that GSDME-mediated pyroptosis may be primarily a pathogenic process rather than an antiviral mechanism during ZIKV infection.
claims.evidence: This is supported by plaque assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing similar viral titers.

claims.claim: Huh-7 and A549 cells showed distinct pyroptotic cell death, elevated LDH levels, and GSDME cleavage upon ZIKV infection.
claims.source: It was observed that Huh-7 and A549 cells showed distinct pyroptotic cell death, elevated LDH levels, and GSDME cleavage upon ZIKV infection, whereas HeLa, HEK-293T, and SH-SY5Y cells exhibited no obvious cytopathic effects even at 72 hr post-infection (Figure 2A-C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy, LDH, and Western blot data in Figures 2A-C.

claims.claim: HeLa, HEK-293T, and SH-SY5Y cells exhibited no obvious cytopathic effects upon ZIKV infection even at 72 hr post-infection.
claims.source: It was observed that Huh-7 and A549 cells showed distinct pyroptotic cell death, elevated LDH levels, and GSDME cleavage upon ZIKV infection, whereas HeLa, HEK-293T, and SH-SY5Y cells exhibited no obvious cytopathic effects even at 72 hr post-infection (Figure 2A-C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy, LDH, and Western blot data in Figures 2A-C.

claims.claim: ZIKV-infected SH-SY5Y cells did not undergo pyroptosis despite expressing a high level of GSDME.
claims.source: However, we noticed that infected SH-SY5Y cells did not undergo pyroptosis despite expressing a high level of GSDME, while Huh-7 and A549 cells expressing the relatively lower GSDME presented the different degrees of pyroptosis and GSDME activation upon infection (Figure 2A-C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that other factors are involved in ZIKV-induced pyroptosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2A-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A showing high GSDME expression but no pyroptosis in SH-SY5Y cells.

claims.claim: JEG-3, Huh-7, and A549 cells displayed the highest susceptibility to ZIKV infection.
claims.source: Among them, JEG-3, Huh-7, and A549 cells displayed the highest susceptibility to ZIKV infection, as assessed by the immunofluorescence assay and the plaque assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and plaque assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: ZIKV-induced LDH release and GSDME activation were enhanced in a virus dose-dependent manner in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: At 24 hr post-infection, the ZIKV-induced LDH release (Figure 2E) and GSDME activation (Figure 2F) were found to be enhanced in a virus dose-dependent manner, which implicit that the productive infection is critical to its pathogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LDH and Western blot data in Figures 2E and 2F showing dose-dependent effects.

claims.claim: Caspase-3 underwent activation and obvious cleavage of GSDME was shown in ZIKV-infected JEG-3 cells at 24 hr post-infection.
claims.source: At 24 hr post-infection, caspase-3 underwent activation and obvious cleavage of GSDME was shown in infected JEG-3 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing caspase-3 activation and GSDME cleavage.

claims.claim: Caspase-3 inhibitor or pan-caspase inhibitor partially prevented ZIKV-induced cell death in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3A and B, ZIKV infection caused the induction of pyroptotic morphological features, and the cell death was partially prevented in the presence of caspase-3 or pan-caspase inhibitors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy and cytotoxicity data in Figures 3A and B showing reduced cell death with inhibitors.

claims.claim: Caspase-3 or pan-caspase inhibitors significantly attenuated the concomitant cleavage of caspase-3 and GSDME in ZIKV-infected JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: In line with these findings, the Western blot analysis revealed that caspase-3 or pan-caspase inhibitors significantly attenuated the concomitant cleavage of caspase-3 and GSDME (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing reduced cleavage with inhibitors.

claims.claim: Treatment of cells with caspase-1 inhibitor and necrosis inhibitor showed no effect on the cell death caused by ZIKV in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: In contrast, the treatment of cells with caspase-1 inhibitor and necrosis inhibitor showed no effect on the cell death caused by ZIKV (Figure 3A-C), which suggests that necrosis and GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis were not involved in it.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3A-C showing no effect of caspase-1 or necrosis inhibitors.

claims.claim: ZIKV infection triggered the activation of both caspase-8 and caspase-9 in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As expected, ZIKV infection triggered the activation of both caspase-8 and caspase-9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), revealing the fact that various biological processes are triggered during ZIKV infection.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing activation of both caspases.

claims.claim: Caspase-8 inhibitor remarkably inhibited the cell membrane rupture, LDH release, and GSDME cleavage in ZIKV-infected JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: It was found that caspase-8 inhibitor remarkably inhibited the cell membrane rupture, LDH release, and GSDME cleavage in infected cells, while inhibition of caspase-9 only slightly inhibited ZIKV-induced activation of GSDME and did not significantly affect ZIKV-induced lytic cell death (Figure 3D-F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), suggesting caspase-8 rather than caspase-9 may play a major role in the activation of caspase-3 and GSDME during ZIKV infection in JEG-3 cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy, LDH, and Western blot data in Figures 3D-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Inhibition of caspase-9 only slightly inhibited ZIKV-induced activation of GSDME and did not significantly affect ZIKV-induced lytic cell death in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: It was found that caspase-8 inhibitor remarkably inhibited the cell membrane rupture, LDH release, and GSDME cleavage in infected cells, while inhibition of caspase-9 only slightly inhibited ZIKV-induced activation of GSDME and did not significantly affect ZIKV-induced lytic cell death (Figure 3D-F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), suggesting caspase-8 rather than caspase-9 may play a major role in the activation of caspase-3 and GSDME during ZIKV infection in JEG-3 cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3D-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D showing minimal effect of caspase-9 inhibitor.

claims.claim: Deletion of caspase-3 completely abolished the ZIKV-induced GSDME-dependent pyroptosis in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3G and H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, the deletion of caspase-3 completely abolished the ZIKV-induced GSDME-dependent pyroptosis, while the deletion of caspase-1 did not affect the ZIKV-induced activation of GSDME and LDH release.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LDH and Western blot data in Figures 3G and H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E showing no pyroptosis in caspase-3 KO cells.

claims.claim: Deletion of caspase-1 did not affect the ZIKV-induced activation of GSDME and LDH release in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3G and H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, the deletion of caspase-3 completely abolished the ZIKV-induced GSDME-dependent pyroptosis, while the deletion of caspase-1 did not affect the ZIKV-induced activation of GSDME and LDH release.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3G and H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E showing no effect of caspase-1 KO.

claims.claim: Knockout of caspase-8 significantly inhibited ZIKV-induced pyroptosis and caspase-3 activation in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As expected, the KO of caspase-8 significantly inhibited ZIKV-induced pyroptosis and caspase-3 activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3G and H showing reduced pyroptosis in caspase-8 KO cells.

claims.claim: ZIKV infection significantly promoted the production of TNF-α in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: To this end, the production of TNF-α in ZIKV-infected or mock-infected JEG-3 cells was determined, which showed that ZIKV infection significantly promoted the production of TNF-α (Figure 3I and J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and ELISA data in Figures 3I and J showing increased TNF-α production.

claims.claim: Blockade of the TNF-α signaling pathway significantly inhibited the ZIKV-induced LDH release and the activation of caspase-8 and GSDME in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: The results showed that blockade of the TNF-α signaling pathway significantly inhibited the ZIKV-induced LDH release and the activation of caspase-8 and GSDME (Figure 3K and L and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that the induction of TNF-α expression contributes to ZIKV-induced pyroptosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LDH and Western blot data in Figures 3K and L and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F showing reduced pyroptosis with TNF-α receptor antagonist.

claims.claim: ZIKV structural proteins are not functional pyroptosis agonists in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: In order to explore which component of the ZIKV is responsible for inducing pyroptosis, JEG-3 cells were infected with ZIKV or UV-inactivated ZIKV to evaluate the contribution of viral structural proteins in inducing the pyroptosis. The results revealed that ZIKV structural proteins are not functional pyroptosis agonists (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B showing no pyroptosis with UV-inactivated ZIKV.

claims.claim: ZIKV NS proteins showed no effect on pyroptosis in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: Then JEG-3 cells were transfected with plasmid encoding individual viral NS proteins to determine the role of NS proteins in activating pyroptosis. However, the NS proteins still showed no effect on pyroptosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D), hence guiding us to speculate that the viral RNA may participate in orchestrating this phenomenon.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D showing no pyroptosis with NS protein expression.

claims.claim: Both 5' and 3' UTRs of ZIKV induced distinct pyroptotic cell death and LDH release in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4A and B, both UTRs induced the distinct pyroptotic cell death and LDH release, and compared to 3' UTR, the 5' UTR caused relatively a stronger effect on inducing pyroptosis (Figure 4A and B), hinting that the recognition of specific viral RNA motifs may aid the GSDME-dependent pyroptosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy and LDH data in Figures 4A and B showing pyroptosis with UTR transfection.

claims.claim: The 5' UTR of ZIKV caused a relatively stronger effect on inducing pyroptosis compared to 3' UTR in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4A and B, both UTRs induced the distinct pyroptotic cell death and LDH release, and compared to 3' UTR, the 5' UTR caused relatively a stronger effect on inducing pyroptosis (Figure 4A and B), hinting that the recognition of specific viral RNA motifs may aid the GSDME-dependent pyroptosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 4A and B showing greater pyroptosis with 5' UTR than 3' UTR.

claims.claim: ZIKV UTRs caused the activation of GSDME via the same signaling pathway as induced by ZIKV infection in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, the Western blot assay demonstrated that the ZIKV UTRs caused the activation of GSDME via the same signaling pathway as induced by ZIKV infection (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4C showing similar pathway activation with UTRs.

claims.claim: Knockdown of RIG-I, but not TLR7 and TLR8, conspicuously attenuated the ZIKV-induced pyroptotic cell death and GSDME cleavage in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: ZIKV infection of engineered or wild-type (WT) cells revealed that the KD of RIG-I, but not TLR7 and TLR8, conspicuously attenuated the ZIKV-induced pyroptotic cell death and GSDME cleavage (Figure 4D-F), suggesting that RIG-I may play a major role in ZIKV-induced pyroptosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy, LDH, and Western blot data in Figures 4D-F showing reduced pyroptosis in RIG-I KD cells.

claims.claim: Deletion of RIG-I significantly inhibited the LDH release and the activation of GSDME, caspase-3, and caspase-8 during ZIKV infection in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4G and H, the deletion of RIG-I significantly inhibited the LDH release and the activation of GSDME, as well as its upstream caspase-3 and caspase-8 during ZIKV infection, while the KO of MDA5 or MAVS only slightly suppressed this process.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LDH and Western blot data in Figures 4G and H showing reduced pyroptosis in RIG-I KO cells.

claims.claim: Knockout of MDA5 or MAVS only slightly suppressed ZIKV-induced pyroptosis in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4G and H, the deletion of RIG-I significantly inhibited the LDH release and the activation of GSDME, as well as its upstream caspase-3 and caspase-8 during ZIKV infection, while the KO of MDA5 or MAVS only slightly suppressed this process.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 4G and H showing minimal effect of MDA5 or MAVS KO.

claims.claim: Deletion of RIG-I suppressed the lytic cell death and the activation of GSDME caused by ZIKV 5' UTR in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: Similarly, we also found that the deletion of RIG-I suppressed the lytic cell death and the activation of GSDME caused by ZIKV 5' UTR (Figure 4I and J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LDH and Western blot data in Figures 4I and J showing reduced pyroptosis in RIG-I KO cells with 5' UTR.

claims.claim: Both poly(I:C) and RIG-IN could activate the lytic cell death and the cleavage of GSDME in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: In order to test this hypothesis, JEG-3 cells were transfected with poly(I:C) (RIG-I agonist) or human RIG-IN (the activation form of RIG-I) construct, and it was found that both poly(I:C) and RIG-IN could activate the lytic cell death and the cleavage of GSDME (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C), indicating that the activation of RIG-I is sufficient to induce GSDME-dependent pyroptosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LDH and Western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C showing pyroptosis with RIG-I activation.

claims.claim: Blocking IFN-I signaling did not affect the 5' UTR-induced GSDME activation in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: JEG-3 cells were treated with a polyclonal antibody against IFNAR1 to block IFN-I signaling, followed by transfection with ZIKV 5' UTR. As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E, blocking IFN-I signaling did not affect the 5' UTR-induced GSDME activation, suggesting that IFN-I response may not be necessary for the activation of ZIKV-induced pyroptosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E showing no effect of IFNAR1 blockade.

claims.claim: Deletion of RIG-I prominently inhibited the ZIKV-induced production of TNF-α in JEG-3 cells.
claims.source: The results showed that the deletion of RIG-I prominently inhibited the ZIKV-induced production of TNF-α (Figure 4K and L), suggesting that RIG-I signaling could promote the production of TNF-α in ZIKV-infected cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and ELISA data in Figures 4K and L showing reduced TNF-α in RIG-I KO cells.

claims.claim: ZIKV infection significantly promoted the LDH release and the GSDME cleavage in mouse primary trophoblast cells (MTCs).
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C, ZIKV infection significantly promoted the LDH release and the GSDME cleavage in MTCs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LDH and Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C showing pyroptosis in MTCs.

claims.claim: Upregulation of RIG-I caused by ZIKV infection was observed in mouse primary trophoblast cells.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous observations in JEG-3 cells, the upregulation of RIG-I caused by ZIKV infection was also seen in MTC, and inhibition of either caspase-3 or caspase-8 prominently blocked ZIKV-induced activation of GSDME (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C showing RIG-I upregulation.

claims.claim: Inhibition of either caspase-3 or caspase-8 prominently blocked ZIKV-induced activation of GSDME in mouse primary trophoblast cells.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous observations in JEG-3 cells, the upregulation of RIG-I caused by ZIKV infection was also seen in MTC, and inhibition of either caspase-3 or caspase-8 prominently blocked ZIKV-induced activation of GSDME (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C showing reduced GSDME activation with inhibitors.

claims.claim: No clinical signs of disease and weight loss were observed in both ZIKV-infected WT and Gsdme-/- dams.
claims.source: Notably, although no clinical signs of disease and weight loss were observed in both ZIKV-infected WT and Gsdme-/- dams (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), most of the WT dams infected with ZIKV showed abnormal pregnancies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, left panel), and their fetuses showed a variable degree of CZS (Figure 5B, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by weight data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A showing no weight loss.

claims.claim: Most of the WT dams infected with ZIKV showed abnormal pregnancies.
claims.source: Notably, although no clinical signs of disease and weight loss were observed in both ZIKV-infected WT and Gsdme-/- dams (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), most of the WT dams infected with ZIKV showed abnormal pregnancies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, left panel), and their fetuses showed a variable degree of CZS (Figure 5B, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B showing abnormal pregnancies in WT dams.

claims.claim: Among all 14 ZIKV-infected WT dams, only 2 dams displayed normal pregnancies.
claims.source: Among all 14 ZIKV-infected WT dams, only 2 dams displayed normal pregnancies.
claims.evidence: This is a direct count from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Out of 109 implantation sites carried by all 14 infected WT dams, 67 (61%) sites were affected, among which 52 showed fetal resorptions and 15 showed growth restriction and malformation.
claims.source: Out of 109 implantation sites carried by all 14 infected dams, 67 (61%) sites were affected, among which 52 showed fetal resorptions and 15 showed growth restriction and malformation (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is a direct count from the experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: The number and severity of affected dams and fetuses were markedly decreased in ZIKV-infected Gsdme-/- dams compared to WT dams.
claims.source: Although ZIKV-infected Gsdme-/- dams also showed a certain degree of abnormal pregnancies, the number and severity of affected dams and fetuses were markedly decreased compared to the WT dams (Figure 5B, C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–2C, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative data in Figures 5B, C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–2C showing reduced adverse outcomes in Gsdme-/- dams.

claims.claim: Among all 10 ZIKV-infected Gsdme-/- dams, only 4 dams showed abnormal pregnancies with a mixture of placental residues and stunted embryonic growth.
claims.source: Among all 10 ZIKV-infected Gsdme-/- dams, only 4 dams showed abnormal pregnancies with a mixture of placental residues and stunted embryonic growth.
claims.evidence: This is a direct count from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The affected fetuses in the ZIKV-infected Gsdme-/- dams were only 18 (20%), which is much lower than that in ZIKV-infected WT dams.
claims.source: The affected fetuses in the ZIKV-infected Gsdme-/- dams were only 18 (20%), which is much lower than that in ZIKV-infected WT dams, Among the 18 affected fetuses, 14 showed fetal resorptions and 4 showed growth restriction and malformation.
claims.evidence: This is a direct count from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Placentas of ZIKV-infected WT dams showed obvious abnormal morphological changes, including hyperplasia, necrosis, and thrombi.
claims.source: While in placentas of ZIKV-infected WT dams, obvious abnormal morphological changes, including hyperplasia, necrosis, and thrombi, were observed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological examination described in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: These pathological changes were not observed in the placentas from ZIKV-infected Gsdme-/- dams.
claims.source: However, these pathological changes were not observed in the placentas from ZIKV-infected Gsdme-/- dams (Figure 5D), suggesting that GSDME is essential to ZIKV-induced placenta pathology.
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological data in Figure 5D showing normal placental morphology in Gsdme-/- dams.

claims.claim: PI-positive signals were detected in the decidua and labyrinth zone in the placentas of ZIKV-infected WT dams.
claims.source: No PI-positive cells were visualized in the placentas of mock-infected dams, while PI-positive signals were detected in the decidua and labyrinth zone in the placentas of ZIKV-infected WT dams.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PI staining data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: The placentas from ZIKV-infected Gsdme-/- dams showed relatively fewer PI-positive signals compared to WT dams.
claims.source: However, the placentas from ZIKV-infected Gsdme-/- dams showed relatively fewer PI-positive signals, implying that GSDME is involved in ZIKV-induced pyroptosis of placentas in vivo (Figure 5E and F).

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2018.

claims.source: Since the NLRP3 inflammasome functions upstream of pyroptosis executor GSDMD and IL-1β is passively released during cell lysis (Jorgensen and Miao, 2015), it can be assumed that pyroptosis may confer ZIKV pathogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Jorgensen and Miao, 2015.

claims.claim: IL-1β is passively released during cell lysis.
claims.source: Since the NLRP3 inflammasome functions upstream of pyroptosis executor GSDMD and IL-1β is passively released during cell lysis (Jorgensen and Miao, 2015), it can be assumed that pyroptosis may confer ZIKV pathogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Jorgensen and Miao, 2015.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wan et al., 2022.

claims.source: It is worth noting that caspase-3 can not only launch pyroptosis by activating GSDME but can also specifically block pyroptosis by cleaving GSDMD at a distinct site from the inflammatory caspases, although the conditions required for this process remain to be further explored (Taabazuing et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Taabazuing et al., 2017.

claims.source: In the case of pyroptosis, caspase-8 is capable of inducing the GSDMD- and GSDME-mediated pyroptosis in murine macrophages (Orning et al., 2018; Sarhan et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Orning et al., 2018; Sarhan et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2019.

claims.source: In addition, caspase-8 inhibits necrosis regulated by receptor-interacting serine/threonine kinase 3 (Tummers and Green, 2017), which fortifies our conclusion that necrosis did not occur in ZIKV-infected JEG-3 cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Tummers and Green, 2017.

claims.source: Recent studies demonstrate that the GSDME-N can permeabilize the mitochondrial membrane and activate the intrinsic apoptotic pathway (Rogers et al., 2019), which implies the possibility that during ZIKV infection, the caspase-8-mediated activation of GSDME consequently induces the caspase-9-associated intrinsic apoptosis by targeting mitochondrial, thereby creating a self-amplifying feed-forward loop through consecutively activating caspase-3.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rogers et al., 2019.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wen et al., 2019; King et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2021.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Pal et al., 2021.

claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated that ZIKV infection activates inflammatory pathways and facilitates the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-1β (IL-1β) in vitro and in vivo (Tappe et al., 2016; He et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Tappe et al., 2016; He et al., 2018.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Jorgensen and Miao, 2015.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Fritsch et al., 2019.

claims.source: Considering that placenta is infected prior to the fetus and that placenta is indispensable for the maternal-fetal nutrient exchange, it is reasonable to speculate that the placental damage during ZIKV infection could be more decisive for adverse fetal outcomes.
claims.evidence: This is based on the understanding of vertical transmission and is supported by the experimental design.

claims.claim: ZIKV is a mosquito-borne flavivirus.
claims.source: Zika virus (ZIKV), a mosquito-borne flavivirus, was initially identified in 1947 but received little concern until it posed a serious public health threat in the Pacific from 2007 to 2015 (Petersen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about ZIKV classification.

claims.claim: Apoptosis is a prototype of programmed cell death (PCD) and is crucial for reproduction, embryonic development, immunity, and viral infections.
claims.source: During ZIKV infection, the placenta can suffer from apoptosis (Miner et al., 2016; Yockey et al., 2018), which is a prototype of programmed cell death (PCD) and is crucial for reproduction, embryonic development, immunity, and viral infections.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about apoptosis.

results.result: ZIKV infection induces GSDME-mediated pyroptosis in JEG-3 placental cells in vitro. ZIKV-infected JEG-3 cells display characteristic pyroptotic morphology (cell swelling, balloon-like structures), release LDH in a time-dependent manner, and show cleavage of GSDME but not GSDMD. Deletion of GSDME suppresses these pyroptotic features without affecting viral replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C31 provide converging evidence from microscopy (pyroptotic morphology), biochemical assays (LDH release, cell viability), and Western blots (GSDME-N cleavage, no GSDMD cleavage). The GSDME-KO rescue experiment (C30-C31) and viral replication data (C32) strengthen the conclusion that GSDME specifically mediates pyroptosis without affecting viral replication. The data are internally consistent and use appropriate controls.

results.result: ZIKV-induced pyroptosis depends on both cellular GSDME abundance and susceptibility to ZIKV infection. Among tested cell lines, Huh-7 and A549 showed pyroptosis with moderate GSDME levels and high ZIKV susceptibility, while SH-SY5Y showed no pyroptosis despite high GSDME expression. JEG-3, Huh-7, and A549 were most susceptible to ZIKV, and pyroptosis was dose-dependent in JEG-3 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 demonstrate that pyroptosis requires both GSDME expression and productive viral infection. The observation that SH-SY5Y cells express high GSDME but don't undergo pyroptosis (C35), combined with susceptibility data (C36) and dose-response experiments (C37), supports a two-factor model. However, the mechanistic basis for why high GSDME alone is insufficient remains unexplored.

results.result: ZIKV activates GSDME through the extrinsic apoptotic pathway via caspase-8 and caspase-3, not through caspase-1 or the intrinsic pathway. Caspase-3 and caspase-8 inhibitors or knockout significantly reduce GSDME cleavage and pyroptosis, while caspase-1 inhibitor/knockout and caspase-9 inhibitor have minimal effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C47 provide strong evidence through pharmacological inhibition (C39-C44) and genetic knockout (C45-C47) approaches. The data consistently show caspase-8 and caspase-3 are required, while caspase-1 and caspase-9 are not essential. The use of both chemical inhibitors and genetic knockouts strengthens the conclusions. However, the partial inhibition by caspase-3 inhibitor (C39) suggests additional complexity not fully explained.

results.result: TNF-α production is induced during ZIKV infection and contributes to pyroptosis through activation of the caspase-8/GSDME pathway. ZIKV infection increases TNF-α mRNA and protein levels, and blocking TNF-α signaling with R-7050 inhibits caspase-8 and GSDME activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 demonstrate TNF-α involvement through expression analysis (RT-qPCR and ELISA) and functional blockade with R-7050. The data show that TNF-α receptor antagonism reduces pyroptosis markers. This connects upstream viral recognition to downstream caspase activation. The mechanistic link is well-supported by the inhibitor data.

results.result: ZIKV genomic RNA, specifically the 5' and 3' UTRs, but not viral structural or NS proteins, induces pyroptosis. Both UTRs induce pyroptotic cell death and GSDME cleavage via the same pathway as live virus, with the 5' UTR showing stronger effects than the 3' UTR.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 systematically exclude viral proteins (UV-inactivated virus, individual NS proteins) and identify viral RNA as the pyroptosis trigger. The UTR transfection experiments (C52-C54) recapitulate the pathway seen with live virus. The differential potency of 5' vs 3' UTR (C53) is interesting but not mechanistically explained. The approach is sound and controls are appropriate.

results.result: RIG-I recognition of ZIKV genomic RNA is the primary sensor triggering pyroptosis, acting independently of IFN-I signaling. RIG-I knockdown or knockout significantly reduces ZIKV-induced pyroptosis, GSDME cleavage, and TNF-α production, while TLR7/8 knockdown and MDA5/MAVS knockout have minimal effects. RIG-I activation alone is sufficient to induce pyroptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C61 provide strong evidence through knockdown (C55), knockout (C56-C58), gain-of-function (C59), and IFN-I blockade (C60) experiments. The data consistently show RIG-I is necessary and sufficient for pyroptosis. The finding that MAVS knockout has minimal effect (C57) suggests a non-canonical RIG-I pathway, which is acknowledged but not fully explained. The connection to TNF-α production (C61) links RIG-I to the downstream caspase pathway.

results.result: ZIKV induces pyroptosis in mouse primary trophoblast cells through the same RIG-I/caspase-8/caspase-3/GSDME pathway observed in JEG-3 cells. ZIKV infection of mouse trophoblast cells increases LDH release and GSDME cleavage, with upregulation of RIG-I and requirement for caspase-3 and caspase-8.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 demonstrate that the mechanism identified in human JEG-3 cells translates to primary mouse trophoblast cells. This is important for validating the in vivo mouse model. The data show similar pathway activation (RIG-I upregulation, caspase dependence, GSDME cleavage). However, the reliance on inhibitors rather than genetic approaches in primary cells is a limitation.

results.result: GSDME ablation in pregnant mice protects against ZIKV-induced adverse fetal outcomes. While ZIKV-infected WT dams showed 61% affected fetuses (52 resorptions, 15 malformations out of 109 sites), Gsdme-/- dams showed only 20% affected fetuses (14 resorptions, 4 malformations out of 90 sites), with no maternal weight loss or clinical signs in either genotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 provide quantitative data from a well-controlled in vivo experiment comparing WT and Gsdme-/- pregnant mice. The reduction in adverse outcomes is statistically significant and biologically meaningful. The lack of maternal symptoms (C65) suggests placental-specific effects. However, the study cannot distinguish maternal vs. fetal GSDME contributions, as acknowledged by the authors. The sample sizes are adequate for the observed effect sizes.

results.result: GSDME is essential for ZIKV-induced placental pathology and pyroptosis in vivo. Placentas from ZIKV-infected WT dams show hyperplasia, necrosis, thrombi, and PI-positive cells in decidua and labyrinth zones, while placentas from Gsdme-/- dams show normal morphology and fewer PI-positive cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 provide histological (H&E staining) and functional (PI staining for membrane permeability) evidence of placental pyroptosis in vivo. The PI staining is an appropriate surrogate for pyroptosis given the lack of effective antibodies for GSDME-N in mouse tissue. The qualitative histological observations are clear, though quantification of pathological features would strengthen the conclusions. The correlation between reduced PI staining and improved fetal outcomes supports causality.

results.result: GSDME ablation does not affect ZIKV replication or tissue distribution in pregnant mice. Comparable viral RNA levels were detected in spleens of WT and Gsdme-/- dams, with no detection in brains or serum, and no significant differences in viral loads in placentas or fetal brains between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 demonstrate that the protective effect of GSDME ablation is not due to reduced viral replication. This is important for establishing that pyroptosis is a pathogenic rather than antiviral mechanism. The qRT-PCR data are appropriate, though viral titers by plaque assay would provide additional confirmation. The lack of brain/serum detection (C77) is consistent with the immunocompetent mouse model used.

results.result: TNF-α receptor antagonist R-7050 treatment protects against ZIKV-induced placental damage and adverse fetal outcomes in pregnant mice. ZIKV infection increases placental TNF-α production, and R-7050 treatment significantly reduces affected fetuses, placental pathology, and pyroptosis compared to vehicle-treated controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 demonstrate therapeutic potential by showing that pharmacological TNF-α blockade recapitulates the protective effect of GSDME knockout. The data include expression analysis (C79), fetal outcome quantification (C80), and histological/PI staining evidence (C81). This validates TNF-α as a therapeutic target. However, the study doesn't address potential effects of R-7050 on maternal immune responses or other TNF-α-dependent processes.

results.result: ZIKV can be transmitted vertically from mother to fetus, causing congenital Zika syndrome (CZS) characterized by microcephaly, growth restriction, and developmental abnormalities through both direct fetal infection and placental damage involving apoptosis and trophoblast dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11-C16 summarize established knowledge from prior literature (supported by multiple citations) that provides context for the current study. These claims accurately represent the scientific consensus on ZIKV pathogenesis and are appropriately cited. They establish the rationale for investigating placental pyroptosis as an additional mechanism.

results.result: Pyroptosis is an inflammatory form of programmed cell death mediated by gasdermin family proteins. GSDMD is cleaved by inflammatory caspases, while GSDME (DFNA5) is cleaved by caspase-3 and granzyme B, and can switch apoptosis to pyroptosis. GSDME was originally identified as a hearing loss gene and tumor suppressor.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22 accurately summarize established knowledge about pyroptosis mechanisms and gasdermin proteins, supported by appropriate citations. This background information is correctly presented and provides necessary context for understanding the novel findings. These are well-established facts in the field.

results.result: Pyroptosis plays important roles in flavivirus pathogenesis. Dengue virus induces NLRP3/GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis in macrophages contributing to hemorrhagic fever, Japanese encephalitis virus induces pyroptosis promoting neuroinvasion, and ZIKV induces caspase-1/GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis in neural progenitor cells contributing to CZS.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 accurately cite prior work on pyroptosis in viral infections, particularly flaviviruses. These citations are appropriate and correctly represent the referenced studies. Claim C25 specifically cites work showing GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis in neural cells, which contrasts with the current study's finding of GSDME-mediated pyroptosis in placental cells, highlighting the novelty of the present work.

results.result: JEG-3 is an appropriate model for studying first-trimester placental ZIKV infection. JEG-3 is a ZIKV-permissive human choriocarcinoma cell line representing trophoblast features, and first-trimester ZIKV infection leads to higher risk of CZS, though mechanisms remain incompletely understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 justify the experimental model choice. C82 is supported by citation to Zachariades et al., 2011, and C83 by citations to Musso and Gubler, 2016; Jagger et al., 2017. The rationale for using JEG-3 cells is appropriate, though the authors acknowledge it's a cancer cell line, which may not fully recapitulate primary trophoblast biology.

results.result: Caspase-3 can be activated through intrinsic (mitochondrial/caspase-9) or extrinsic (death receptor/caspase-8) apoptotic pathways, and GSDME-mediated pyroptosis can occur downstream of both pathways. TNF-α activates death receptor signaling and caspase-8, while RIG-I and TLR7/8 sense viral ssRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 accurately summarize established cell death and innate immunity mechanisms, supported by appropriate citations. This background knowledge is correctly presented and provides necessary context for interpreting the experimental findings. These are well-established principles in the field.

results.result: The choice of immunocompetent pregnant mouse model is justified because IFN-I signaling plays important roles in ZIKV pathogenesis and placental development, and ZIKV infection in immunocompetent pregnant mice causes placental damage and adverse fetal outcomes without maternal symptoms. Prior work suggests placental pathology may be more important than direct fetal infection for adverse outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 justify the experimental model choice with appropriate citations. The rationale for using immunocompetent rather than immunocompromised mice is sound, as it preserves physiological immune responses. The citations support the claims about IFN-I roles (C93), lack of maternal symptoms (C94), and importance of placental pathology (C95). C96 provides supporting evidence that caspase-3 inhibition doesn't affect brain pathology in a different model.

results.result: ZIKV and other viruses can induce GSDME-mediated pyroptosis with varying pathogenic consequences. ZIKV NS proteins activate NLRP3 inflammasome, H7N9 influenza and enterovirus 71 induce pathogenic GSDME pyroptosis, SARS-CoV-2 induces GSDME pyroptosis in syncytia, while some viruses trigger GSDME pyroptosis as an antiviral mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C103 accurately cite recent literature on GSDME in viral pathogenesis, providing context for the current findings. The citations are appropriate and correctly represent the referenced work. These claims establish that GSDME-mediated pyroptosis is an emerging theme in virology, with both pathogenic and antiviral roles depending on context.

results.result: Caspase-3 and caspase-8 have complex roles in cell death. Caspase-3 can both activate GSDME to induce pyroptosis and cleave GSDMD to inhibit pyroptosis. Caspase-8 can induce GSDMD/GSDME pyroptosis in macrophages and inhibit necroptosis. GSDME-N can permeabilize mitochondria and activate intrinsic apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 accurately cite literature on the multifunctional roles of caspases and GSDME in cell death pathways. These citations are appropriate and provide important context for understanding the complexity of the pathways studied. The bidirectional relationship between apoptosis and pyroptosis is well-established in the cited literature.

results.result: R-7050 is a TNF-α receptor antagonist that has shown therapeutic efficacy in multiple disease models and inhibits caspase-8 and caspase-3 activation by blocking TNF-α signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 accurately describe R-7050 based on cited literature (Wen et al., 2019; King et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2021; Pal et al., 2021). The characterization of the compound and its mechanism is appropriate and provides justification for its use in the therapeutic experiments. The citations support both the compound's properties and prior therapeutic applications.

results.result: Background information on ZIKV biology, pyroptosis detection methods, and placental function.
